content: Drug-drug interactions are so named because, in addition to the effects rifamycins have on protease inhibitors and NNRTIs (non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors), antiretroviral agents can also influence the blood levels of rifamycins. Updated data on these interactions and recommendations for their use have been provided by CDC scientists and external expert consultants. Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs), such as zidovudine, didanosine, zalcitabine, stavudine, lamivudine, and abacavir, are not metabolized by the CYP450 enzyme system. Therefore, concurrent use of NRTIs and rifamycins is not contraindicated and does not require dose adjustments. Previously, rifabutin was recommended as the preferred alternative to rifampin for treating active tuberculosis (TB) in patients taking protease inhibitors or NNRTIs. Rifampin was specifically contraindicated for patients on any protease inhibitors or NNRTIs, while rifabutin was contraindicated for those taking ritonavir or delavirdine. New data suggest that rifampin can be used to treat active TB in three specific scenarios: 1. In patients whose antiretroviral regimen includes the NNRTI efavirenz and two NRTIs. 2. In patients whose regimen includes the protease inhibitor ritonavir and one or more NRTIs. 3. In patients whose regimen includes a combination of two protease inhibitors (ritonavir and either saquinavir hard-gel or soft-gel capsules). Updated guidelines recommend significantly reducing the dose of rifabutin (to 150 mg two or three times per week) when co-administered with ritonavir (with or without saquinavir) and increasing the dose of rifabutin (to 450–600 mg daily or 600 mg two or three times per week) when used with efavirenz. Among protease inhibitors, ritonavir has the highest potency in inhibiting CYP450. At low doses, ritonavir combined with saquinavir significantly increases saquinavir blood levels. However, the complexity of drug interactions increases when two protease inhibitors are used together. Co-administration of saquinavir soft-gel capsules (SGC) with usual-dose rifabutin (300 mg daily or two or three times per week) is possible, but pharmacokinetic data and clinical experience are limited. Similarly, the combination of saquinavir (SGC or hard-gel capsules) and ritonavir with either usual-dose rifampin (600 mg daily or two or three times per week) or reduced-dose rifabutin (150 mg two or three times per week) is a possibility, though data are limited. Co-administration of saquinavir (SGC or hard-gel capsules) with rifampin (without ritonavir) is not recommended due to a marked decrease in saquinavir concentrations. If ritonavir and rifabutin are used together, a substantially reduced rifabutin dose (150 mg two or three times per week) is recommended. Co-administration of ritonavir with usual-dose rifampin (600 mg daily or two or three times per week) is possible, but pharmacokinetic data and clinical experience are limited. There is limited but favorable clinical experience with co-administration of indinavir and a reduced daily dose of rifabutin (150 mg) or the usual dose of rifabutin (300 mg two or three times per week). However, co-administration of indinavir with rifampin is not recommended due to a marked decrease in indinavir concentrations. Similarly, limited but favorable clinical experience exists for co-administration of nelfinavir with a reduced daily dose of rifabutin (150 mg) or the usual dose of rifabutin (300 mg two or three times per week). Co-administration of nelfinavir with rifampin is not recommended because rifampin markedly decreases nelfinavir concentrations. Co-administration of amprenavir with a reduced daily dose of rifabutin (150 mg) or the usual dose of rifabutin (300 mg two or three times per week) is a possibility, but no published clinical experience exists. Co-administration of amprenavir with rifampin is not recommended due to a marked decrease in amprenavir concentrations. Co-administration of nevirapine with usual-dose rifabutin (300 mg daily or two or three times per week) is possible based on pharmacokinetic data, but no published clinical experience exists. Data are insufficient to determine whether dose adjustments are necessary when rifampin is co-administered with nevirapine. Therefore, rifampin and nevirapine should only be used together if clearly indicated and with careful monitoring. Co-administration of delavirdine with either rifabutin or rifampin is contraindicated due to a marked decrease in delavirdine concentrations. Co-administration of efavirenz with increased-dose rifabutin (450–600 mg daily or 600 mg two or three times per week) is a possibility, though no published clinical experience exists. Similarly, co-administration of efavirenz with usual-dose rifampin (600 mg daily or two or three times per week) is a possibility, but no published clinical experience exists. For protease inhibitors such as amprenavir, nevirapine, delavirdine, and efavirenz, usual recommended doses are 400 mg twice daily for each protease inhibitor and 400 mg of ritonavir.
